metadata.title: Data Sufficiency for Time and Distance
metadata.description: Decide whether motion data are enough to produce one definite answer, without doing unnecessary calculation.
metadata.teachingApproach: Teach sufficiency as a uniqueness test, not a full-solution contest. Cover both-together cases, I-alone and II-alone cases, either-alone sufficiency, insufficiency even after combining, early/late conditions that need pairing, equal-distance average questions where scale cancels, and three-statement redundancy. For each case, show exactly what remains unknown before deciding.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 18, Time and Distance, including its Data Sufficiency exercise. Approved scope: Teach the chapter's sufficiency outcomes using speed ratios, route time, distance, early/late travel, average speed, relative speed and redundant statements. Learners should test each statement independently first, combine only when necessary, and decide whether the answer is unique.

content.text:
Let's learn Data Sufficiency for Time and Distance.

The goal is not to solve more than necessary. Ask only: do the given statements fix one definite answer?

Suppose X and Y cover the same route.
I. Their speeds are in the ratio 3 : 4.
II. Y takes 36 minutes.

I gives only a relationship. II gives only Y's time.

Together they are enough.

Same distance → time ratio X : Y = 4 : 3.
If Y takes 36 min, X takes 48 min.

So this is a “both together only” case.

How long does P take for a route?
I. P : Q speed = 2 : 5.
II. Q takes 30 minutes for the same route.
Which is sufficient?

inlineData.prompt:
How long does P take for a route?
I. P : Q speed = 2 : 5.
II. Q takes 30 minutes for the same route.
Which is sufficient?
hints: I gives only a ratio; II gives only Q's time.
Together, time ratio P : Q = 5 : 2.
inlineData.explanation: Neither statement alone fixes P's time. Together, 2 time-parts = 30, so P takes 75 min. Both together only.

content.text:
Let's check this clue.

I gives only a ratio; II gives only Q's time.

Neither statement alone fixes P's time. Together, 2 time-parts = 30, so P takes 75 min. Both together only.

Now use that idea on a new question.

How long does A take for a route?
I. A : B speed = 4 : 7.
II. B takes 28 minutes for the same route.
Which is sufficient?

inlineData.prompt:
How long does A take for a route?
I. A : B speed = 4 : 7.
II. B takes 28 minutes for the same route.
Which is sufficient?
hints: Reverse the speed ratio to get time ratio 7 : 4.
Both facts are needed to turn the ratio into minutes.
inlineData.explanation: I alone has no absolute time; II alone has no relation to A. Together A takes 49 minutes, so both are necessary.

content.text:
Let's work through this one.

I alone has no absolute time; II alone has no relation to A. Together A takes 49 minutes, so both are necessary.

Try the question once more and check each clue.

Sometimes one statement already contains distance and speed.

Question: How long for 180 km?
I. Speed is 60 km/hr.
II. Departure is at 9 a.m.

I alone gives time = 180/60 = 3 hr.
II tells only a clock time, not a travel rate.

So I alone is sufficient.

How long will a car take to cover 240 km?
I. Its speed is 80 km/hr.
II. It starts at 7:30 a.m.
Which is sufficient?

inlineData.prompt:
How long will a car take to cover 240 km?
I. Its speed is 80 km/hr.
II. It starts at 7:30 a.m.
Which is sufficient?
hints: Distance is already in the question.
Statement I gives the missing speed.
inlineData.explanation: 240/80 = 3 hr from I alone. Starting time does not affect travel duration, so I alone is sufficient.

content.text:
Let's check this clue.

Distance is already in the question.

240/80 = 3 hr from I alone. Starting time does not affect travel duration, so I alone is sufficient.

Now use that idea on a new question.

How long will a bus take to cover 150 km?
I. Its speed is 50 km/hr.
II. It leaves after sunrise.
Which is sufficient?

inlineData.prompt:
How long will a bus take to cover 150 km?
I. Its speed is 50 km/hr.
II. It leaves after sunrise.
Which is sufficient?
hints: I gives speed, and the question gives distance.
II gives no numerical travel information.
inlineData.explanation: I alone gives 150/50 = 3 hr. Statement II is irrelevant.

content.text:
Let's work through this one.

I alone gives 150/50 = 3 hr. Statement II is irrelevant.

Try the question once more and check each clue.

A statement can hide enough information to recover both speed and route length.

Suppose a jogger runs 80 minutes on the same route daily.
A statement says: 5 miles by 5:40 and 8 miles by 6:04.

That statement shows 3 miles in 24 minutes.
At constant speed, 80 minutes covers 3 × 80/24 = 10 miles.

A separate statement giving only the start time adds nothing.

A jogger runs at a constant speed for 90 minutes. How long is the route?
I. The jog starts at 5:00 p.m.
II. Between 5:20 and 5:50 the jogger covers 4 km.
Which is sufficient?

inlineData.prompt:
A jogger runs at a constant speed for 90 minutes. How long is the route?
I. The jog starts at 5:00 p.m.
II. Between 5:20 and 5:50 the jogger covers 4 km.
Which is sufficient?
hints: II gives 4 km in 30 minutes, so it gives the speed.
The 90-minute total duration is already in the question.
inlineData.explanation: II gives speed = 8 km/hr. In 1.5 hr the route is 12 km. I alone gives no speed, so II alone is sufficient.

content.text:
Let's check this clue.

II gives 4 km in 30 minutes, so it gives the speed.

II gives speed = 8 km/hr. In 1.5 hr the route is 12 km. I alone gives no speed, so II alone is sufficient.

Now use that idea on a new question.

A cyclist rides at a constant speed for 2 hours. How far?
I. The ride begins at 6 a.m.
II. The cyclist covers 15 km in 30 minutes.
Which is sufficient?

inlineData.prompt:
A cyclist rides at a constant speed for 2 hours. How far?
I. The ride begins at 6 a.m.
II. The cyclist covers 15 km in 30 minutes.
Which is sufficient?
hints: II gives speed = 30 km/hr.
The question already gives 2 hours.
inlineData.explanation: II alone gives distance = 30 × 2 = 60 km. Start time is not needed.

content.text:
Let's work through this one.

II alone gives distance = 30 × 2 = 60 km. Start time is not needed.

Try the question once more and check each clue.

Sometimes either statement can independently lead to the answer.

Question: A 120-mile round trip is made at one uniform speed. How long does it take?
I. Speed is 30 mph.
II. At 10 mph faster, the trip would take 3 hours.

I alone: 120/30 = 4 hr.
II alone: 120/(v+10)=3 gives v=30, then time = 4 hr.

Each statement works independently — an “either alone” case.

A 180 km trip is made at a uniform speed. How long does it take?
I. Speed is 60 km/hr.
II. At 30 km/hr faster, the trip would take 2 hours.
Which description is correct?

inlineData.prompt:
A 180 km trip is made at a uniform speed. How long does it take?
I. Speed is 60 km/hr.
II. At 30 km/hr faster, the trip would take 2 hours.
Which description is correct?
hints: Test I and II separately.
II gives v + 30 = 90, so v = 60.
inlineData.explanation: I alone gives 180/60 = 3 hr. II alone also gives v = 60 and hence 3 hr. Either statement alone is sufficient.

content.text:
Let's check this clue.

Test I and II separately.

I alone gives 180/60 = 3 hr. II alone also gives v = 60 and hence 3 hr. Either statement alone is sufficient.

Now use that idea on a new question.

A 200 km trip is made at a uniform speed. Find its time.
I. Speed is 50 km/hr.
II. At 50 km/hr faster, the trip would take 2 hours.
Which description is correct?

inlineData.prompt:
A 200 km trip is made at a uniform speed. Find its time.
I. Speed is 50 km/hr.
II. At 50 km/hr faster, the trip would take 2 hours.
Which description is correct?
hints: I gives time directly.
II gives v + 50 = 100, so v = 50.
inlineData.explanation: Both statements independently lead to v = 50 km/hr and time = 4 hr. Either alone is sufficient.

content.text:
Let's work through this one.

Both statements independently lead to v = 50 km/hr and time = 4 hr. Either alone is sufficient.

Try the question once more and check each clue.

Two statements can still be insufficient if too many unknowns remain.

Question: distance between two towns?
I. Mail train is 12 km/hr faster than express.
II. Mail takes 40 minutes less.

Unknowns include mail speed, express speed and distance.
The two relationships do not fix one unique distance.

So even both statements together are insufficient.

What is the distance between two towns?
I. A car is 15 km/hr faster than a bus.
II. The car takes 30 minutes less than the bus.
Which is sufficient?

inlineData.prompt:
What is the distance between two towns?
I. A car is 15 km/hr faster than a bus.
II. The car takes 30 minutes less than the bus.
Which is sufficient?
hints: There are still three unknown quantities: two speeds and the distance.
Two relationships allow many possible distance-speed pairs.
inlineData.explanation: The two statements relate the unknowns but do not fix an absolute speed or distance. Even together they are insufficient.

content.text:
Let's check this clue.

There are still three unknown quantities: two speeds and the distance.

The two statements relate the unknowns but do not fix an absolute speed or distance. Even together they are insufficient.

Now use that idea on a new question.

Find the route length.
I. Runner A is 3 km/hr faster than runner B.
II. A takes 20 minutes less for the route.
Which is sufficient?

inlineData.prompt:
Find the route length.
I. Runner A is 3 km/hr faster than runner B.
II. A takes 20 minutes less for the route.
Which is sufficient?
hints: No absolute speed or time is given.
Different speed pairs can satisfy both statements with different route lengths.
inlineData.explanation: Both statements still leave multiple solutions, so the data are insufficient even together.

content.text:
Let's work through this one.

Both statements still leave multiple solutions, so the data are insufficient even together.

Try the question once more and check each clue.

An early/late statement can supply the missing time difference only when paired with a speed-change statement.

A 150 km trip is 30 minutes late at usual speed; increasing speed by 25 km/hr makes it on time.

Let usual speed be v.

150/v − 150/(v+25) = 1/2.
This fixes v uniquely.

The distance, speed change and delay must all work together.

What is a train's usual speed?
I. Increasing speed by 25 km/hr lets it cover a 150 km route on time.
II. At usual speed it is 30 minutes late.
Which is sufficient?

inlineData.prompt:
What is a train's usual speed?
I. Increasing speed by 25 km/hr lets it cover a 150 km route on time.
II. At usual speed it is 30 minutes late.
Which is sufficient?
hints: I alone does not say how much time must be saved; II alone gives no speed change.
Together form 150/v − 150/(v+25) = 1/2.
inlineData.explanation: The equation gives v = 75 km/hr. Neither statement alone fixes v, so both together are necessary.

content.text:
Let's check this clue.

I alone does not say how much time must be saved; II alone gives no speed change.

The equation gives v = 75 km/hr. Neither statement alone fixes v, so both together are necessary.

Now use that idea on a new question.

What is a car's usual speed?
I. Increasing speed by 20 km/hr lets it cover a 120 km route on time.
II. At usual speed it is 30 minutes late.
Which is sufficient?

inlineData.prompt:
What is a car's usual speed?
I. Increasing speed by 20 km/hr lets it cover a 120 km route on time.
II. At usual speed it is 30 minutes late.
Which is sufficient?
hints: Each statement alone is missing a key relation.
inlineData.explanation: Together the statements give v = 60 km/hr. Both are necessary.

content.text:
Let's work through this one.

Together the statements give v = 60 km/hr. Both are necessary.

Try the question once more and check each clue.

Data Sufficiency is about information, not always absolute numbers.

For four equal-distance stretches, the speeds alone can determine average speed because the common distance cancels.

If the speeds are 10, 20, 30 and 60 km/hr, choose 60 km each.
Times are 6, 3, 2 and 1 hr.
Total 240 km in 12 hr → average 20 km/hr.

No total distance or total time is needed.

What is the average speed over four equal-distance stretches?
I. Speeds are 12, 24, 24 and 48 km/hr.
II. Total journey time is 10 hours.
Which is sufficient?

inlineData.prompt:
What is the average speed over four equal-distance stretches?
I. Speeds are 12, 24, 24 and 48 km/hr.
II. Total journey time is 10 hours.
Which is sufficient?
hints: Equal distances are already stated in the question.
With I, choose any common distance and total the times.
inlineData.explanation: I alone determines the average because the common distance cancels. II alone gives total time but no distance or speeds.

content.text:
Let's check this clue.

Equal distances are already stated in the question.

I alone determines the average because the common distance cancels. II alone gives total time but no distance or speeds.

Now use that idea on a new question.

What is the average speed over three equal-distance stretches?
I. Speeds are 20, 30 and 60 km/hr.
II. The trip begins at noon.
Which is sufficient?

inlineData.prompt:
What is the average speed over three equal-distance stretches?
I. Speeds are 20, 30 and 60 km/hr.
II. The trip begins at noon.
Which is sufficient?
hints: Choose 60 km for each stretch using I.
Start time does not determine average speed.
inlineData.explanation: I alone gives times 3, 2 and 1 hr for 180 km, so average = 30 km/hr. II is irrelevant.

content.text:
Let's work through this one.

I alone gives times 3, 2 and 1 hr for 180 km, so average = 30 km/hr. II is irrelevant.

Try the question once more and check each clue.

Three-statement questions often ask which information is redundant.

Suppose:
I. A moves at 40 km/hr.
II. B moves at 50 km/hr.
III. B is 10 km/hr faster than A.

Any two statements recover both speeds:
I + II gives them directly.
I + III gives B = 50.
II + III gives A = 40.

So any one statement can be dropped.

To find the relative speed of A and B moving in opposite directions:
I. A moves at 24 km/hr.
II. B moves at 36 km/hr.
III. B is 12 km/hr faster than A.
Which is true?

options.label: Any one statement can be dropped

inlineData.prompt:
To find the relative speed of A and B moving in opposite directions:
I. A moves at 24 km/hr.
II. B moves at 36 km/hr.
III. B is 12 km/hr faster than A.
Which is true?

options.label: Any one statement can be dropped

hints: Test I+II, I+III, and II+III separately.
Every pair determines both individual speeds, so their sum can be found.
inlineData.explanation: I+II give 24 and 36 directly. I+III gives B = 36. II+III gives A = 24. Any one statement is redundant.

content.text:
Let's check this clue.

Test I+II, I+III, and II+III separately.

I+II give 24 and 36 directly. I+III gives B = 36. II+III gives A = 24. Any one statement is redundant.

Now use that idea on a new question.

To find the relative speed of P and Q moving in the same direction:
I. P moves at 45 km/hr.
II. Q moves at 60 km/hr.
III. Q is 15 km/hr faster than P.
Which is true?

options.label: Any one statement can be dropped

inlineData.prompt:
To find the relative speed of P and Q moving in the same direction:
I. P moves at 45 km/hr.
II. Q moves at 60 km/hr.
III. Q is 15 km/hr faster than P.
Which is true?

options.label: Any one statement can be dropped

hints: Any two statements recover both speeds.
Then same-direction relative speed is the difference.
inlineData.explanation: Each pair fixes P = 45 and Q = 60, so any one statement can be dropped. Their relative speed is then 15 km/hr.

content.text:
Let's work through this one.

Each pair fixes P = 45 and Q = 60, so any one statement can be dropped. Their relative speed is then 15 km/hr.

Try the question once more and check each clue.

You can now judge a Time and Distance question before doing unnecessary work.

Ask what the question needs, test each statement alone, and combine only if necessary. A statement is sufficient only when it fixes one definite answer.

That completes Topic 18. The next chapter, Boats and Streams, keeps the same relative-speed idea but adds the current of the water.
